## Open

### T-166 — Self-registration has no approval or verification step

> _2026-09-27 · realm/blong-access · open_

access.registration.add creates an account that is active immediately with the Guest role: there is
no pending state, no email verification and no approval queue anywhere in blong-access or
blong-party. If the intended product behaviour is that a self-registered account waits for an
operator, the realm needs a state on access.user (or a credential policy) that the session gate
consults, plus a way for an operator to approve it - access.user.edit exists, but nothing marks such
accounts as awaiting approval, so an operator cannot tell a self-registered account from a seeded
one except by its creation time. Decided as D-300: the account must prove its email address before
the session gate will use it, skipped only for social logins whose verified email claim the provider
already vouches for. Delivery settled as D-302: expose access.registration.verify and let the suite
wire the sender, so the realm owns the state and the gate and not an SMTP client.

Sized on 2026-09-28, and deliberately left as one pass rather than started as a fragment:
access.user gains the verification state (a NOT NULL column needs a default, or existing rows fail
on the next schema sync, so it arrives with one and the seeds set it explicitly),
access.registration.add writes the unverified state and issues a token, a new
access.registration.verify consumes the token, and the refusal lands where the credential is checked
(access.credential.check, which login already calls) as a typed error. The blast radius is the
seeds: every seeded account in every suite must come out verified, or the integration suites stop
logging in - so the sequence is schema and seeds first, then the handler, then the refusal, with the
login flow test as the guard.

### T-176 — The capability spec's action pivot still ticks row one

> _2026-09-28 · realm/blong-access · open_

capability.play.ts declares its action detail pivot with no filters, so
`fields: {find: true, add: true}` lands on whichever action `access.action` lists first — a list
that grows with every test-created action, which makes the capture drift and its checkmark
meaningless. Apply the same treatment as role.play.ts's capability pivot: add `filter: true` to the
action name column in accessCapabilityModel.ts, name the action the spec means in the detail's
filters, and regenerate that spec's captures in the same run. Check the other pivots too:
matrix.play.ts filters targetName and user.play.ts filters roleName, so those two are the ones that
already name their row.

### T-177 — An edge with an unknown object id is dropped silently

> _2026-09-29 · realm/blong-access · open_

syncEdges inserts its edges with onConflict().ignore(), which MySQL turns into INSERT IGNORE, and
INSERT IGNORE downgrades a foreign-key violation to a warning: submitting a role id that does not
exist reports success and writes nothing. That is the same silent-skip shape as the ghost resource
of T-102, in the write direction, and it is worth closing — by resolving the submitted ids before
the insert and raising the realm's own typed error for an unknown one, rather than by dropping the
ignore (the ignore is what makes two edits racing on the same subject harmless). It also means the
rollback of a realm add or edit cannot be tested by submitting a bad id: the statement that would
have failed never raises, so a test for the transaction needs a different injected failure — and
while the point of T-177 was the transaction rather than this, a test that proves a failure rolls
the credentials back is still missing.

### T-179 — Three access handlers still write the ensure and the matrix separately

> _2026-09-29 · realm/blong-access · open_

accessRoleAdd, accessRoleEdit and accessCapabilityAdd call core.resource.ensure and then write their
edges or ACL matrix on the pool, with no transaction around either, so a failure between them leaves
a capability with no actions or a role with no rules — the shape T-177 closed everywhere else. The
blocker is that super cannot reach a member of the caller's own group, and accessRoleAdd's path goes
through accessRoleEnsure in the same realm, so a transaction there needs a mechanism other than
delegation — passing the transaction through the port in-process, which is safe only because every
realm's db layer is attached to the single srv.db port, or inlining the ensure into roleAdd with
super. Now that coreResourceEnsure takes a transaction, whichever is chosen is small.

### T-198 — The access short-type map must learn a new table's kind

> _2026-10-04 · realm/blong-access · open_

SHORT_TYPE_ALIASES in realm/blong-access/adapter/db/accessModel.ts maps the short names an ACL
declaration may use (person, unit, organization, user, role, capability, action, all) to full
core_type aliases. A rule for any other table has to name the full alias, because an unmapped value
is taken verbatim and a short name like consent resolves to a type alias nobody registered, which
fails at seed time with 'references an unknown consent'. The workaround is documented in the party
matrix seed. The design question is whether a product realm should be able to extend the map, since
a shared realm cannot know the tables of the products it ships with, and the alternative — naming
the full alias everywhere — makes the ACL seeds the one place that already knows the realm's type
naming.

### T-450 — access.user.edit refuses an edit that only touches roles

> _2026-10-27 · realm/blong-access · open_

access.user.edit cannot be used to change only a user's roles or credentials: it calls the generic
super.exec first, and with a user object that carries nothing but userId knex refuses with "Empty
.update() call detected". Granting a role therefore forces the caller to also send a column it did
not want to change (isActive, say), which the model screens always do and a scripted call does not.
The fix is to skip the generic update when the submitted user object has no columns beyond the id,
then run the credential, role and matrix sync as it does now; add a case to realm/blong-access tests
that edits roles alone.

### T-451 — No UI page calls access.profile.password.change

> _2026-10-27 · realm/blong-access · open_

The portal ships no page that calls access.profile.password.change, so a deployed user cannot change
their own password: the handler and its policy enforcement exist in realm/blong-access
(currentPassword + newPassword, minLength from access.policy) but no model or component exposes it.
blong-dev user passwd is the operator-side workaround; the gap is a profile/password page or a
button on the user's own profile screen, wired to that method. Check first whether
core/blong-browser's profile page pattern already has a slot for it, and add a Playwright capture of
the flow so the page is proven to reach the handler.

### T-370 — Make the authorization flow runnable from the Test runs page

> _2026-10-18 · realm/blong-access · done_

The console catalog first listed only the session flow. testAuthorizationFlow.ts used Buffer, which
a browser page does not have, and its first step assumed no MLE token and expected a 401, which a
signed-in portal makes impossible. It was made browser-safe with Uint8Array and atob and host-aware
for the pre-login assertions, then added back to accessTestRunCatalog and the testGroups map. Both
flows are browser-safe and host-aware; the access spec captures the session and authorization runs.

### T-371 — Give the server test runner a gateway dispatch port

> _2026-10-18 · realm/blong-access · done_

The server runner lives in realm/blong-test (orchestrator/testRun/testRunner.ts,
orchestrator/testDispatch.ts, gateway/test validations, server/testRunController.ts). The blocker
was on the browser side: the remote.bindingFailed error was created by core/blong-gogo/src/Remote.ts
in sender(), reached from _getMethod/busMethod and the browser handlerProxy; the ui realm Remote
used by useBlong().handler had no sender for test.run.start. The resolution is the backend route:
the browser page calls backend/test.run.*, the backend adapter strips the prefix, the gateway
validations expose the methods, and the blong-test testDispatch port runs the group. Access
Playwright captures the server-hosted run.
